title: Simple in-order cores over complex out-of-order cores for throughput workloads
decision: Designed simple, in-order, single-issue cores with no out-of-order execution, no speculative execution, minimal pipeline stages — in favor of having many cores and threads per chip
alternatives_or_rejected: Complex out-of-order superscalar core (high single-thread performance approach)
rationale: Server workloads are dominated by threads with memory-level parallelism; complex cores leave much of their transistor budget and pipeline capability unused on such workloads; simpler cores deliver better aggregate throughput per watt and per die area
outcome: Niagara achieved high throughput on commercial server workloads; single-thread performance was lower than competing high-IPC designs but aggregate throughput was competitive or superior
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly lists out-of-order as a considered and rejected alternative, or whether it simply argues for the simple approach without framing it as a formal rejection of OoO; the paper_vs_general is high because this philosophy is well-attested in the paper, but explicit 'we considered X and rejected it' language may not be there

title: 8-core, 4-threads-per-core organization (32 total threads) as the core/thread balance point
decision: Chose 8 cores with 4 strands (threads) each rather than either fewer more-complex cores or many more simpler threads
rationale: 4 threads per core allowed the pipeline to be kept simple while hiding memory latency; 8 cores provided enough thread-level parallelism to keep the memory system busy; die area and power constraints bounded the total; this balance was driven by target workload characteristics (commercial server, database, web)
outcome: Effective latency hiding; high utilization of the fetch/execute pipeline across diverse thread counts; marketed as a 32-way multithreaded processor
weakest_point: The exact number 8×4 may be right but I am not 100% certain the paper explicitly states this specific trade-off rationale rather than just describing the architecture; the number itself (32 threads total) is definitely in the title and paper, but whether alternatives (e.g., 16 cores × 2 threads) were explicitly discussed is less certain

title: Throughput-over-single-thread-performance as the primary design philosophy
decision: Optimized the design explicitly for aggregate throughput on multi-threaded workloads rather than single-thread peak performance
rationale: Most server processor utilization is low because threads stall on memory; the best way to improve server performance is to improve throughput across many threads, not peak single-thread IPC; this is framed as a fundamental philosophy driving all other decisions
outcome: Niagara succeeded in markets where thread count and memory bandwidth mattered more than single-thread speed; it underperformed on single-threaded and latency-sensitive workloads
weakest_point: While the philosophy is strongly present in the paper, I'm uncertain whether it is stated as an explicit decision episode (we chose X over Y) or simply as a design philosophy framing throughout; the quote field is 'cannot-reproduce-verbatim' because I cannot recall a specific sentence verbatim even though the spirit is clear

title: Shared L2 cache across all cores rather than private L2 per core
decision: Implemented a shared 3MB L2 cache accessible by all 8 cores rather than private L2 per core
rationale: Workload working sets vary across threads; a shared cache allows better utilization of the cache capacity across heterogeneous thread behavior; simplifies coherency; shared L2 with 8 ports or banked structure supports aggregate throughput goals
outcome: Shared cache achieved good utilization across diverse thread working sets; coherency protocol remained manageable
weakest_point: I believe the paper discusses shared vs. private cache tradeoffs but am not certain it explicitly frames shared L2 as a chosen alternative versus a private-L2 design that was considered and rejected; the shared cache description is definitely in the paper but the 'alternatives' framing may be my inference
